clinician.trajectory_summary: A 58-year-old woman presented with progressive lower extremity numbness, paresthesias, and mild weakness following a COVID-19 infection. Initially, her neurological exam showed normal strength and reflexes. However, within 24 hours, her condition deteriorated with worsening weakness (3/5 in lower extremities, 4/5 in left upper extremity) and diminished deep tendon reflexes, prompting suspicion of GBS. An urgent lumbar puncture revealed CSF findings of albumin-cytologic dissociation, with a white cell count of 2 cu/mm and a protein count of 117 mg/dL. MRI of the lumbar spine showed an unremarkable conus medullaris, effectively ruling out significant spinal cord pathology as the primary cause of her symptoms.

key_supporting_evidence.claim: Patient developed worsening weakness (3/5 in lower extremities, 4/5 in left upper extremity) and diminished deep tendon reflexes within 24 hours of admission, indicating neurological deterioration consistent with GBS progression.
CSF analysis from lumbar puncture showed albumin-cytologic dissociation with a white cell count of 2 cu/mm and a protein count of 117 mg/dL, a hallmark finding of GBS.
MRI of the lumbar spine showed an unremarkable conus medullaris, ruling out significant spinal cord compression or pathology as the cause of symptoms.

ruled_out_or_less_likely_alternatives.basis: While MRI showed some neural foraminal narrowing, the rapid ascending weakness, diminished reflexes, and CSF albumin-cytologic dissociation are more consistent with GBS, and the conus medullaris was unremarkable (E005).
MRI of the lumbar spine explicitly stated an 'unremarkable conus medullaris' (E005).

remaining_uncertainties: Findings from nerve conduction studies (NCS) and electromyography (EMG) to electrophysiologically confirm GBS.
